meta.title: Stem, Inc. (NYSE: STEM) — Arun Narayanan's Software Pivot: From Hardware Reseller to AI-Driven Energy Dispatch Platform, Athena's Rebirth as PowerTrack, and the Race to Recurring Revenue Amid a Stressed Balance Sheet

chapters.title: Strategic Snapshot: The Software Wager at the Edge of the Grid
chapters.body:
## A Company Remade, a Balance Sheet Unchanged

Stem, Inc. entered the spring of 2026 carrying two very different financial identities simultaneously. On one measure, the ~~San Francisco-based~~ ==Houston-based== energy software company had achieved what its prior management had promised for years but never delivered: a genuine software gross margin. The GAAP gross margin on its core business reached 38 percent in fiscal year 2025, reversing from negative 7.6 percent in FY2024 — a swing of more than 45 percentage points that validated the hardware-exit thesis management had staked the company's future on. On another measure, Stem remained what its SPAC-era balance sheet had made it: a company carrying ~~$548 million~~ ==$547.8 million== in total liabilities against ~~$309 million~~ ==$281.9 million== in total assets, with $36.6 million in unrestricted cash as of March 31, 2026 — enough to fund operations for roughly three to four quarters at its current burn rate of $8 to $12 million per quarter.

The tension between those two realities is the central strategic fact of Stem's story in 2026.

## Narayanan's Mandate

The pivot point came on January 27, 2025, when Arun Narayanan stepped in as chief executive officer, replacing interim CEO David Buzby. Narayanan arrived from the industrial digital sector — 21 years at SLB, a stint as Chief Data Officer at Anglo American, and most recently CEO of RES Digital Solutions — carrying a mandate to complete what the 2024 strategy reset had begun: strip out the hardware-heavy revenue that had consumed capital and suppressed margins, and prove that what remained was a durable software business.

On the fourth-quarter 2025 earnings call, Narayanan described the year in terms that acknowledged the distance traveled while quietly sidestepping the distance still to go:

> "2025 was a transformative year that methodically yet decisively reshaped STEM into a software centric, operationally disciplined organization."

'Transformed' in this context carried specific operational content: a 27 percent workforce reduction in April 2025, $24 million in partial-year cost savings, and the June 2025 debt exchange that retired approximately $350 million of existing convertible notes in exchange for $155 million of new 11 percent first-lien senior secured notes due December 2030. What it did not mean was that the balance sheet had been made whole. Working capital remained negative by approximately $16 million. Stockholders' equity stood at negative $265.9 million. The accumulated deficit reached approximately $1.49 billion.

## Three Numbers, One Thesis

Three quantitative anchors define the investment proposition as of the frozen snapshot date of May 2026:

| Metric | Value | Context |
|---|---|---|
| Annual Recurring Revenue | $61.1M | +16% year-over-year |
| Adjusted EBITDA (FY2025) | $6.7M | First-ever positive reading |
| Cash on hand (Q1 2026) | $36.6M | -$12.3M in the quarter |

The ARR figure — representing subscription and managed services revenue that recurs independently of hardware shipments — is the numerator in the software-transition argument. The $6.7 million adjusted EBITDA for FY2025 was the first positive reading in the company's history, accompanied by the first positive operating cash flow of $6.9 million. Both milestones confirmed that the cost structure, having absorbed the April 2025 reductions and the wind-down of hardware procurement, was now smaller than the gross profit the software base could generate.

The cash figure is where the thesis meets its constraint. At $8 to $12 million of quarterly cash consumption, $36.6 million buys perhaps three quarters of independent operation — less if revenue conversion lags or if PowerTrack EMS bookings, the key FY2026 growth driver, arrive later than anticipated. Management established a $30 million at-the-market equity program in March 2026 as an explicit liquidity backstop, signaling that dilutive capital raises remain a live scenario.

## The IRA Catalyst and the Race to Monetize

Against that cash clock, Stem is attempting to capture a structural tailwind: the Inflation Reduction Act's domestic content provisions and storage investment tax credits have accelerated a 2026–2027 utility-scale battery buildout that represents the largest single addressable market expansion in the company's history. PowerTrack EMS — the standalone and hybrid energy storage management system launched September 2, 2025 — was purpose-built to serve this market, competing at the grid edge for the next generation of large battery deployments that IPPs and utilities are now actively commissioning.

The company's central strategic wager, then, is timing: that IRA-driven storage procurement will generate recognizable PowerTrack EMS revenue by late 2026 or early 2027, pulling ARR toward the $65–70 million management guidance range for year-end 2026 and narrowing the gap toward the $100-million-plus threshold that would demonstrate durable software scale. What Stem cannot control is how quickly the grid interconnection queue clears, how rapidly independent power producers sign software agreements ahead of project completion, or whether political headwinds to IRA implementation intensify.

Stem's margin story is genuinely new. Its balance sheet is genuinely old. The next twelve months will establish which one is determinative.

chapters.title: Corporate History: From Powergetics to SPAC-Fueled Ambition to the 2024 Reset
chapters.body:
## Origins: Machine Learning Meets the Demand Charge

Stem, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware on March 16, 2009, under the name Powergetics. Its founding proposition was deceptively simple but technically ambitious: commercial and industrial buildings pay enormous demand charges — utility penalties levied on peak electricity consumption within any fifteen-minute window — and a sufficiently intelligent battery system, positioned behind the meter, could shave those peaks automatically and profitably. The company's earliest years were spent developing Athena, a machine-learning dispatch engine designed to ingest real-time pricing signals, weather forecasts, and historical load patterns and translate them into continuous, automated charge-and-discharge decisions.

For most of its first decade, Stem operated as a developer-financed energy-as-a-service provider. Rather than selling batteries to customers outright, it acquired storage hardware, placed the systems at commercial sites under long-term offtake contracts, and monetised value through Athena's dispatch optimisation — a model that bundled the physical asset with the intelligence layer. The approach gained traction in California's demand-charge-intensive commercial sector before the company broadened geographically and began bidding battery assets into utility ancillary-services markets. By the late 2010s, the core thesis — that software-optimised energy storage could generate durable recurring revenue — was proving out at the unit level, even if the balance sheet remained capital-hungry.

## The SPAC Window Opens — and Stem Steps Through

The clean-energy SPAC wave of 2020–2021 presented a faster path to the public markets and the growth capital to accelerate. On April 28, 2021, Stem completed a business combination with Star Peak Energy Transition Corp., a blank-check vehicle, raising ~~approximately $525 million~~ ==over $600 million== in gross proceeds. The transaction valued the combined company at ~~just over $2 billion~~ ==approximately $1.35 billion in pro forma equity value at the announced $10.00 per Star Peak share== — a premium that embedded expectations of rapid software subscription growth, not merely battery deployment.

Wall Street's enthusiasm reflected a genuine thesis: a capital-light software layer atop an expanding installed base of energy storage assets could compound on falling hardware costs while building a moat through switching costs in Athena's optimisation models. But the public-market debut also committed Stem to a quarterly cadence of disclosure that would eventually expose the structural tensions between its hardware-heavy revenue trajectory and the recurring-revenue story management was selling to investors.

## The AlsoEnergy Bet — $695 Million for a Customer Base

Six months after listing, Stem made the most consequential decision of its corporate history. ~~In January 2022~~ ==On February 1, 2022==, it acquired AlsoEnergy Holdings for ~~approximately $695 million, paid entirely in stock~~ ==an announced $695 million — roughly 75% cash and 25% stock, with a final purchase price of approximately $652.0 million==, adding roughly 16,000 commercial and industrial solar monitoring customers and a cloud-based SaaS platform that tracked performance across more than 30 gigawatts of installed capacity in over 50 countries.

The strategic logic was defensible. AlsoEnergy's monitoring software — sold as a subscription to solar developers, O&M contractors, and asset owners — gave Stem a recurring-revenue base that was immediately accretive to the software story. Bundling solar monitoring with battery dispatch optimisation created a unified operations layer: a customer who used AlsoEnergy's platform to watch their panels could, in theory, be upsold Athena for a co-located storage system. The combined entity would serve the full asset lifecycle for commercial solar-plus-storage projects.

What was less defensible was the price. The ~~$695 million~~ ==$652 million== acquisition, transacted at the peak of growth-equity valuations when Stem itself briefly carried a market capitalisation exceeding $2 billion, looked visionary in early 2022. By early 2026, Stem's market cap had contracted to approximately $93 million. The implied goodwill written into that acquisition — hundreds of millions of dollars for a SaaS platform that would eventually be rebranded PowerTrack — proved impossible to sustain as interest rates rose, energy storage project timelines slipped, and Stem's own hardware-resale strategy began generating thin margins at scale.

## The Hardware Ramp and the Structural Trap

Following the AlsoEnergy acquisition, Stem's revenue trajectory accelerated sharply — but through a channel that carried its own detonator. To capitalise on a boom in utility-scale battery procurement driven by state renewable mandates and falling lithium-ion costs, Stem expanded aggressively into battery hardware resale, sourcing systems from manufacturers and bundling them into integrated solar-plus-storage project contracts. Revenue grew from $111 million in FY2021 to $461.5 million in FY2023, making Stem look, superficially, like a company scaling rapidly.

The reality was more troubling. Hardware resale margins are structurally thin — often in the low single digits — and the working-capital dynamics are punishing: Stem had to procure batteries months before projects reached commissioning, creating a large contract-liability pile that deferred revenue recognition while cash went out the door. Interconnection delays — the chronic failure of grid operators to process connection applications fast enough to match the pace of project development — created violent revenue-timing cliffs: a project expected to close in one quarter would slip into the next or beyond, leaving recognised revenue below contract value while costs continued accumulating. By the end of FY2023, Stem carried a cumulative deficit exceeding $1.6 billion.

The structural flaw was not hidden; it was embedded in the business model. Hardware resale required Stem to compete with battery distributors and EPC contractors on price while simultaneously funding the SaaS overlay that justified its premium valuation. The margin profiles of these two businesses pointed in opposite directions, and the market was beginning to notice.

## 2024: The Collapse

The reckoning arrived in 2024. In August of that year, NYSE notified Stem that its 30-day average stock price had fallen below $1.00, triggering a potential delisting review — a disclosure that crystallised, in a single regulatory letter, how far the company had fallen from its 2021 ambitions. Simultaneously, management slashed full-year 2024 revenue guidance from an original midpoint near $617 million to what would eventually settle as $144.6 million in actuals, a 69-percent contraction year-over-year. The causes were enumerated in filings: interconnection delays on hardware projects, USDA funding lags on rural energy programmes, and — critically — the deliberate decision to exit large-scale battery hardware resale as a primary business line.

The [FY2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=STEM&type=10-K), filed under going-concern disclosures, was unambiguous about the company's financial condition. Stem entered 2025 with ~~$548 million~~ ==approximately $835.2 million== in total liabilities against ~~$309 million~~ ==approximately $437.4 million== in total assets, negative working capital of approximately $16 million, and a convertible note stack whose maturity profile posed an existential question if software revenue growth did not accelerate.

The board moved quickly. David Buzby, who had been serving as interim chief executive, stepped aside on January 27, 2025, when Arun Narayanan was appointed. Narayanan brought a profile unlike any prior Stem CEO: 21 years at SLB (formerly Schlumberger) in software and data leadership, followed by the role of Chief Data Officer at Anglo American and then Chief Digital Officer at RES. His mandate was explicit — reposition Stem as an AI-driven software company and arrest the cash burn before the balance sheet forced resolution on someone else's terms.

## The Debt Exchange: Buying Time to Prove the Thesis

The financial condition created an immediate constraint on Narayanan's strategy. Stem carried approximately $350 million of convertible notes whose maturity structure would have forced a reckoning within any realistic software-ramp horizon. On June 30, 2025, the company completed a debt exchange transaction that retired ==most of== that note stack in exchange for $155 million of new 11 percent First Lien Senior Secured Notes due December 2030 plus $10 million in cash. Outstanding principal fell by approximately $195 million, and ~~all material debt maturities were pushed past 2028~~ ==the bulk of remaining maturities were extended into 2030, though the company's 0.50% convertible notes due December 2028 remained outstanding after the exchange==.

The exchange did not make Stem solvent in any conventional sense — the new notes carry an 11 percent interest rate that consumes cash at a rate no $61-million ARR base can cover unaided. But it created the temporal conditions for the current strategy to be tested on its merits: a multi-year window in which the PowerTrack platform must demonstrate that commercial solar monitoring, AI dispatch optimisation, wholesale-market bidding, and utility-scale storage control can compound into a recurring revenue base that justifies the capital structure above it.

The transition from Powergetics — a behind-the-meter battery aggregator founded in Delaware in 2009 — to a debt-restructured AI energy software company ~~in San Francisco~~ ==headquartered in Houston== in 2025 is a story of genuine technological ambition meeting serial misjudgements in capital allocation and acquisition timing. The Athena engine that Stem's engineers built over a decade was never the problem. The question, now arriving with real urgency, is whether what surrounds it — the balance sheet, the restructured platform, and a new chief executive — can catch up.

chapters.title: Products and Platforms: The PowerTrack Architecture and the Utility-Scale Expansion
chapters.body:
The platform Stem, Inc. operated by mid-2026 bore little structural resemblance to the single-product dispatch engine that had defined the company's early reputation. Between 2022 and 2025, through acquisition, in-house development, and deliberate brand consolidation, Stem assembled a five-product software stack under the PowerTrack name — a suite designed to manage solar and battery assets from performance monitoring through daily dispatch through wholesale market participation. CEO Arun Narayanan framed the ambition in broad terms, describing the goal as making Stem

> "the operating system for new energy projects across solar, storage, and hybrid assets."

Whether that vision was achievable — and on what timeline — depended heavily on how each product layer fed the others, and what it would cost a customer to disentangle them.

## The Platform Architecture: Five Products, One Data Spine

PowerTrack was best understood as a layered stack rather than a monolithic platform. At its foundation sat PowerTrack Asset Performance Management (APM), the solar monitoring and analytics layer Stem acquired when it purchased AlsoEnergy Holdings for ~~approximately $695 million in stock in January 2022~~ ==a final purchase price of approximately $652 million (announced at $695 million with roughly 75% cash and 25% stock) in a transaction that closed February 1, 2022==. APM ingested real-time and historical performance data from solar inverters, sensors, and meters across approximately 30 gigawatts of capacity in more than 50 countries — the raw telemetry stream that every other PowerTrack module depended upon.

Sitting above APM was PowerTrack Optimizer, the storage dispatch engine tracing its lineage to Athena, the machine-learning algorithm Stem had built in-house beginning around 2016. Optimizer ingested asset telemetry from APM, layered in real-time wholesale electricity pricing, demand-charge tariff structures, weather forecasts, and asset degradation models, and issued automated dispatch instructions for battery systems managing approximately 2 gigawatt-hours of capacity. The optimization logic ran continuously, recalibrating dispatch schedules as market conditions shifted intraday.

PowerBidder Pro extended the stack into wholesale market participation, enabling community choice aggregators, independent power producers, and renewable developers to bid storage and solar generation directly into organized electricity markets for energy arbitrage and ancillary services revenue. The signing of Mercuria — the global commodity trading firm, which standardized a second renewable portfolio on PowerBidder Pro in Texas during 2025 — signaled that sophisticated financial operators regarded Stem's dispatch modeling as fit for trading-desk standards.

PowerTrack Sage, ~~rolled out to the full customer base by Q4 2025~~ ==in beta with more than 80 customers as of Q4 2025, with general availability expected at the end of March 2026 and a lite version rolling out across the customer base at launch==, served as the AI assistant layer spanning the entire suite. It provided natural-language querying of asset data, anomaly detection alerts, and predictive maintenance recommendations — reducing the analyst hours required to surface an underperforming inverter string or model a dispatch scenario, and ==positioned to reinforce== ~~reinforcing~~ platform stickiness by embedding workflow dependency directly into the operator interface.

The compounding effect of these integrations was where switching costs accumulated. A C&I operator using APM, Optimizer, and PowerBidder Pro — all feeding from a common data model accessible through the Sage interface — faced a migration exercise proportional to its multi-product adoption depth. Custom alert thresholds, historical performance baselines, dispatch optimization configurations, and wholesale bidding strategies were all stored and contextualized within the Stem environment. Moving off one product meant re-engineering the dependencies of the others.

## The Athena Rebrand: Repositioning or Reinvention?

In 2025 Stem retired the Athena name, folding the dispatch engine into the unified PowerTrack brand as PowerTrack Optimizer. Cosmetically, "Athena" had accumulated limiting connotations — a behind-the-meter, C&I product from a company that once owned the batteries it dispatched. The PowerTrack umbrella provided a brand architecture that enterprise buyers and utility procurement teams could evaluate as a coherent software platform rather than a collection of acquired point tools.

Technically, the rebrand coincided with meaningful product consolidation. The AlsoEnergy APM platform and the legacy Athena dispatch engine had operated on separate code bases and separate customer portals for nearly three years after the 2022 acquisition. The PowerTrack unification brought them onto a common data model and a single customer interface — a change with real operational value for the substantial portion of Stem's customer base managing both solar and storage assets simultaneously. Whether the underlying optimization algorithm itself changed materially was less clear from public disclosures; Stem described the brand evolution more than the engineering changes behind it, and the rebrand's most visible effect was go-to-market rather than computational.

## PowerTrack EMS: Entering the Utility-Scale Arena

The most consequential product development of 2025 was the September 2 launch of PowerTrack EMS, a standalone and hybrid energy storage management system targeting utility-scale battery deployments. The product addressed a technical problem that PowerTrack Optimizer — designed for behind-the-meter commercial environments — was not built to solve: managing front-of-meter battery systems at multi-hundred-megawatt scale, where software must interface with grid operators in real time, comply with FERC Order 2222 aggregation requirements, and execute grid-scale ancillary service obligations with sub-second response capability.

The competitive landscape at utility scale was substantially more demanding than the C&I segment. Stem's principal adversaries were Fluence — the Siemens-AES joint venture whose Mosaic platform had been deployed at gigawatt-scale across the United States and internationally — and Tesla Autobidder, integrated natively with Tesla's Megapack hardware.

| Platform | Owner | Hardware dependency | Deployment scale as of 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fluence Mosaic | Siemens / AES JV | Hardware-agnostic in principle | Multi-GW deployed globally |
| Tesla Autobidder | Tesla, Inc. | Optimized for Megapack | Large US / international installed base |
| PowerTrack EMS | Stem, Inc. | Hardware-agnostic | ~~First contract: Nebraska BESS, 2025~~ ==First publicly disclosed utility-scale selection: Everyray, 100 MWh, Germany, March 2026== |

Stem's differentiation argument rested on its software-only, hardware-agnostic positioning. Having exited battery hardware resale at scale, the company could credibly present PowerTrack EMS as a neutral control layer — a pitch with genuine appeal to utility developers and IPPs who had made multi-vendor hardware procurement decisions and had no strategic interest in ceding software control to a battery manufacturer. Fluence's Mosaic, despite its own hardware-agnostic claims, operated within a corporate structure where hardware and software revenue both accrued to the parent consortium. Tesla's Autobidder optimization was calibrated around Megapack systems.

The vulnerability in Stem's positioning was capitalization. Fluence could draw on the engineering resources of two Fortune 500 parents; Tesla cross-subsidized Autobidder development against hardware margin. Stem, carrying $548 million in total liabilities and a $36.6 million cash position as of March 31, 2026, was attempting to build out a utility-scale software category against substantially better-resourced incumbents. Management was explicit that meaningful revenue recognition from PowerTrack EMS would not arrive until late 2026 or early 2027 — a timeline reflecting both the project-finance-driven development cycle for utility-scale storage, where projects typically take 18 to 36 months from contract to commissioning, and the enterprise procurement cycles at regulated utilities. ~~The company's first standalone BESS contract in Nebraska validated the sales motion without yet moving financial metrics.~~ ==The company's first publicly disclosed utility-scale selection — Everyray's 100 MWh Germany announcement on March 4, 2026 — validated the sales motion without yet moving financial metrics.==

## raicoon GmbH: The First International Product Bet

~~In Q1 2026~~ ==On April 23, 2026 (announced April 28)==, Stem acquired Vienna-based raicoon GmbH for $4.3 million in stock ==(389,569 shares of Stem common stock)== — a transaction modest by any financial measure but significant as the company's first deliberate international product investment. raicoon had developed solar energy management software tailored to European regulatory frameworks, including VAT-specific reporting requirements, European grid interconnection standards, and the country-level net metering and feed-in tariff structures that differed materially from US utility tariff design. Its customer base consisted primarily of European solar installers, small commercial operators, and community energy projects — a natural adjacency to the monitoring and optimization customers Stem already served through AlsoEnergy's European monitoring contracts.

The acquisition augmented a Berlin competence center that Stem had established as its EMEA expansion anchor. European renewable developer Everyray had signed a 100 MWh ~~partnership in 2025~~ ==partnership announced March 4, 2026==, providing the region's first meaningful reference customer. raicoon extended the platform's addressable market to smaller European solar operators who required localized compliance features that a US-built product could not readily serve without dedicated regional engineering — precisely the gap the Vienna team had been built to fill.

## Platform Defensibility: The Metrics Case

By early 2026, the installed base metrics underpinning Stem's software narrative had reached a scale that was genuinely difficult for a new entrant to replicate. Approximately 16,000 commercial and industrial customers used PowerTrack APM for solar monitoring, representing 30 gigawatts under management across more than 50 countries. Thirteen of the top 15 US commercial and industrial solar operators ran on the platform, and the company claimed approximately 70 percent share of the US C&I solar software market. Ninety percent of leading US community solar asset owners operated on Stem's platform.

That penetration created data density that made Stem's optimization algorithms progressively more accurate: more asset-hours of dispatch data improved the machine-learning models informing PowerTrack Optimizer's pricing and degradation assumptions. It also created contractual inertia. A mid-market solar operator whose operations team had spent three years building alert hierarchies, custom reports, and integration workflows atop PowerTrack APM faced a migration cost that was economically meaningful even if a competitor offered a marginally superior product.

The $61.1 million ARR base that management reported at year-end 2025, growing 16 percent year-over-year, represented the financial crystallization of that installed-base stickiness. The challenge was that stickiness maintained the base — it did not grow it fast enough to reach the $100 million ARR threshold that would demonstrate durable software scale while servicing 11 percent senior secured notes. PowerTrack EMS was meant to supply that growth. The question the balance sheet had made urgent was whether the utility sales cycle would move quickly enough to answer it.

chapters.title: Financial Deep Dive: The Margin Inflection, the Debt Burden, and the Cash Clock
chapters.body:
## Revenue Trajectory: Collapse, Then Rebuild

The revenue chart for Stem, Inc. tells two stories inside the same data series. Between FY2020 and FY2023, total revenue expanded from $36.3 million to $461.5 million — a twelve-fold surge that accompanied every SPAC-era narrative about clean energy hypergrowth. What that trajectory concealed was that the growth was driven overwhelmingly by battery hardware resale, a low-margin pass-through business that added bulk to the income statement while ~~compressing GAAP gross margins below zero for five consecutive years~~ ==pushing GAAP gross margins below zero in FY2020 and again, after the wind-down began, in FY2024==. When the hardware business was wound down deliberately beginning in 2024, the income statement finally told the truth.

| Fiscal Year | Total Revenue | Core Revenue | Hardware Resale | GAAP Gross Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2020 | $36.3M | not separately disclosed | not separately disclosed | -10.8% |
| FY2021 | $127.4M | not separately disclosed | not separately disclosed | n/a |
| FY2022 | $363.0M | not separately disclosed | not separately disclosed | n/a |
| FY2023 | $461.5M | not separately disclosed | not separately disclosed | n/a |
| FY2024 | $144.6M | ~$113M (est.) | ~$32M (est.) | -7.6% |
| FY2025 | $156.3M | $141.4M | ~$14.9M | 38.4% |
| Q1 2026 | $29.0M | not separately disclosed | not separately disclosed | 37.4% |

The [FY2024 revenue contraction to $144.6 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001758766/000175876625000005/stem-20241231.htm) — a 69 percent decline year-over-year — was the product of choosing margins over scale. The underlying software and services core represented $141.4 million of the $156.3 million total in FY2025, up 25 percent year-over-year. Battery hardware resale contributed the remaining roughly $15 million in FY2025, guided to return to approximately $40 million in FY2026 on an opportunistic basis, which creates the unusually wide FY2026 guidance range of $140 to $190 million. The [Q1 2026 revenue of $29.0 million](https://investors.stem.com/news/news-details/2026/Stem-Announces-First-Quarter-2026-Results/default.aspx) — implying an annualized run-rate of roughly $116 million if extrapolated — reflected an 11 percent year-over-year decline as hardware wound down faster than software bookings converted to recognised revenue.

## The Gross Margin Inflection

The financial thesis at Stem centres on one data series: GAAP gross margin. In FY2020, the company reported a margin of negative 10.8 percent. ~~That figure remained negative for five consecutive fiscal years, reaching~~ ==Gross profit turned positive in FY2021, FY2022, and FY2023 on the strength of the hardware-led revenue surge, before slipping back to== negative 7.6 percent in FY2024 even as the hardware exit was underway. The turn came in FY2025, and it was not a gradual improvement but a step-change.

[Full-year 2025 GAAP gross profit reached $60.0 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001758766/000175876626000014/exhibit99-8xkx20260304xq42.htm) on $156.3 million of revenue, up from negative $11.1 million in FY2024. Three cost-of-revenue line items drove the shift.

Hardware cost-of-revenue, which had historically represented 60 to 80 percent of total cost of revenue in peak years, effectively disappeared from the ongoing business. Battery hardware sold at or near cost — sometimes below — generating negative contribution margin at scale, and its exit removed the single largest weight on the income statement. Second, software amortisation from the ~~$695 million~~ ==$652 million== AlsoEnergy acquisition continues to step down on schedule through intangible asset expiration dates concentrated in the 2025–2030 window, easing the cost-of-revenue charge incrementally each period. Third, the April 2025 workforce reduction — approximately 27 percent of the global headcount, from roughly 480 employees to 350, at a restructuring charge of $6.1 million — targeted $24 million in partial-year 2025 savings and approximately $30 million in annualised FY2026 savings, flowing directly into services gross margin in the second half of the year.

By Q1 2026, GAAP gross margin held at 37.4 percent. Management's FY2026 guidance calls for non-GAAP gross margins of 40 to 50 percent, implying the business is approaching software-comparable margin profiles as hardware resale is bounded and services scale.

## Deconstructing FY2025: The Headline and the Reality

Stem reported a GAAP net income of $137.8 million for FY2025 — the first positive net income in the company's history, against an accumulated deficit of approximately $1.49 billion. The figure demands careful interpretation.

The dominant driver was a ~~non-cash debt extinguishment gain of approximately $195 million~~ ==non-cash debt extinguishment gain of $220.0 million== recorded when the June 30, 2025 notes exchange retired roughly $350 million of existing convertible notes in exchange for $155 million of new 11 percent First Lien Senior Secured Notes due December 2030 and $10 million in cash. Under GAAP, the ~~$195 million~~ ==$220.0 million== difference between the extinguished liability and the fair value of the new instrument passes through the income statement as a gain.

Strip out that gain, and the picture changes materially. The operating loss for FY2025 was approximately $55 million. The company's first-ever positive adjusted EBITDA of $6.7 million and its first-ever positive operating cash flow of $6.9 million are genuine milestones that validate the margin thesis — but they represent the economics of the restructured business at its current scale, not a company capable of organically servicing $342 million of remaining debt principal. The FY2025 GAAP net income is best read as a balance-sheet event, not an operating achievement.

## The Capital Structure: Three Instruments, One Constraint

The June 2025 debt exchange materially extended Stem's maturity runway, but the liability profile remains deeply stressed. As of [Q1 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001758766/000175876626000043/exhibit99-8xkx20260506xq12.htm), total liabilities stood at $547.8 million against total assets of ~~$308.9 million, implying $238.9 million~~ ==$281.9 million, implying $265.9 million== of net liability excess. Stockholders' equity was negative $265.9 million.

| Instrument | Principal | Coupon | Maturity | Est. Annual Cash Interest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.50% Convertible Notes | $68M | 0.50% | Dec 2028 | ~$0.3M |
| 4.25% Convertible Notes | $119M | 4.25% | Apr 2030 | ~$5.1M |
| 11% First Lien Senior Secured Notes | $155M stated / $134M FV | 11% cash or 12% PIK | Dec 2030 | ~$17.1M (if cash elected) |
| **Total** | **~$342M** | | | **~$22.5M** |

The 0.50 percent convertible notes mature in December 2028 — approximately 30 months from the frozen snapshot date. At the current ARR trajectory of $61.1 million growing 16 percent annually, ARR would reach ~~roughly $83 million by year-end 2028, still well short of a level that would comfortably retire a $68 million tranche without refinancing or equity support~~ ==about $82.2 million by year-end 2027 and about $95.4 million by year-end 2028 — recurring software revenue, not free cash flow, leaving retirement of the $68 million tranche dependent on refinancing or equity support== . The 4.25 percent convertible notes due April 2030 create a second maturity wall at $119 million, carrying an annual cash coupon of approximately $5.1 million.

The most consequential instrument is the 11 percent First Lien Senior Secured Notes. Cash interest at 11 percent on $155 million is approximately $17.1 million per year. If management elects the PIK option to preserve liquidity, the coupon rises to 12 percent and compounds the principal: $155 million becomes approximately $174 million after a single year of PIK election, worsening the eventual refinancing challenge. The aggregate annual cash interest burden at stated rates, assuming no PIK election across all three instruments, approaches $22.5 million — a figure that alone represents more than three-quarters of Q1 2026's total revenue.

## The Cash Clock

The cash flow evolution across recent periods renders the strategic timeline with arithmetic precision.

| Period | Operating Cash Flow | Quarter-End Cash |
|---|---|---|
| FY2024 | -$36.7M | n/a |
| FY2025 | +$6.9M | ~$48.9M (est.) |
| Q1 2026 | -$8.3M | $36.6M |

Cash declined $12.3 million in Q1 2026 — combining the $8.3 million operating outflow with investing and financing activity — leaving $36.6 million on the balance sheet as of March 31, 2026. If the Q1 quarterly cash decline of $12.3 million persisted for four consecutive quarters, the implied annual erosion would be approximately $49 million, exhausting existing liquidity in roughly three quarters. Management has asserted that cash covers at least 12 months of operations under the base case — credible, but conditioned on significant second-half 2026 revenue weighting from PowerTrack EMS deployments, PIK election on the senior notes to avoid the $17.1 million cash coupon, and working capital stability. The negative working capital of approximately $16 million as of Q1 2026 provides no buffer against a slip in that sequencing.

## The ATM: Dilution Signal, Not Yet Drawn

The $30 million at-the-market equity programme established in March 2026 is best read as explicit acknowledgment that the cash constraint is real. With no shares issued by quarter-end, it remained undrawn at the frozen snapshot date — but its establishment signals that management and the board have pre-positioned for scenarios where organic cash generation cannot bridge the gap between the current liquidity position and the December 2028 convert maturity.

At Stem's market capitalisation of approximately $93 million, a full $30 million ATM draw would represent approximately 32 percent dilution to existing shareholders. The threshold scenario in which the ATM remains undrawn requires ARR to compound at 20 percent or better annually — reaching $90 to $100 million by FY2027 — alongside PowerTrack EMS beginning to generate material recognised revenue before mid-2027 and PIK election preserving cash through 2026. The scenario in which it is partially or fully drawn materialises if hardware resale timing disappoints, EMS revenue recognition slips past year-end, or the IRA-driven utility-scale storage buildout is delayed by interconnection constraints that have already burned Stem once.

The financial story of Stem in mid-2026 is ultimately a question of timing rather than thesis. The margin inflection is structurally real: a 48-point improvement in GAAP gross margin from negative 10.8 percent to positive 38.4 percent over five fiscal years is not noise. Annual recurring revenue of $61.1 million growing at 16 percent reflects a sticky and expanding installed base of 16,000 C&I solar customers and approximately 2 gigawatt-hours of storage under dispatch. But the cash clock runs concurrently with the growth story, and the $155 million of senior secured debt at 11 to 12 percent annual interest is indifferent to how compelling the software narrative sounds. Whether the ARR base compounds fast enough to service that debt before the balance sheet forces the issue is the central, unresolved question the Q3 and Q4 2026 results will begin to answer.

chapters.title: Valuation: Distressed Equity or Emerging Software Multiple — the Range of Plausible Outcomes
chapters.body:
## The Valuation Problem: When Standard Metrics Break Down

Stem, Inc. entered the second quarter of 2026 as a company that conventional equity valuation frameworks cannot easily digest. At $9.72 per share and an implied market capitalisation of approximately $93 million as of early May 2026, the stock offered neither a coherent price-to-earnings ratio — the company posted a $14.2 million operating loss in Q1 2026 alone — nor a meaningful price-to-book figure. With stockholders' equity reported at negative $265.9 million as of 31 March 2026, the book-value denominator is not merely unhelpful but directionally misleading: a company with negative book equity trading at a positive share price is, by definition, pricing in optionality that balance-sheet accounting cannot capture. The relevant valuation vocabulary here belongs to software and recurring-revenue analytics: enterprise value relative to annual recurring revenue, gross profit, and trailing sales — multiples that speak to the durability and scalability of the software stack rather than the inherited liabilities of the hardware reseller Stem once was.

## Computing Enterprise Value and Current Multiples

Reconstructing Stem's enterprise value at the May 2026 snapshot requires adding gross debt to market capitalisation and netting available cash. Total indebtedness stood at approximately $321 million: $68 million in 0.50% convertible notes due December 2028, $119 million in 4.25% convertible notes due April 2030, and roughly $134 million fair value of the new 11% first-lien senior secured notes due December 2030, issued in the June 2025 exchange transaction. Against a $93 million equity market cap and [$36.6 million of cash on hand as of 31 March 2026](https://investors.stem.com/news/news-details/2026/Stem-Announces-First-Quarter-2026-Results/default.aspx), the implied enterprise value was approximately **$377 million**.

Against that EV, the relevant multiples at the frozen snapshot read as follows:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| EV / FY2025 Revenue (~$156M) | 2.4x |
| EV / FY2026 Guided Revenue (midpoint $165M) | 2.3x |
| EV / FY2025 GAAP Gross Profit ($60M) | 6.3x |
| EV / FY2025 ARR ($61.1M) | 6.2x |
| EV / FY2026 Forward ARR (guide midpoint $67.5M) | 5.6x |
| EV / FY2025 Adj. EBITDA ($6.7M) | 56x |
| P/E ratio | Not meaningful (sustained net operating losses) |
| Price-to-book | Not meaningful (negative stockholders' equity) |

The 56x EV/Adjusted EBITDA is not a signal that investors are paying a growth premium commensurate with a high-flying SaaS company — it simply reflects how thin the [first-ever positive adjusted EBITDA of $6.7 million for FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001758766/000175876626000014/exhibit99-8xkx20260304xq42.htm) is relative to a $377 million enterprise value. The most informative multiples at this stage are EV/ARR and EV/Gross Profit, which isolate the recurring software economics the investment thesis hinges on, and EV/Revenue, which contextualises total activity including opportunistic hardware resale.

## Peer Context

Benchmarking Stem against public comparables illuminates the gap between where the stock trades today and where a clean software re-rating would place it. The peer set spans two distinct clusters: clean energy software platforms and distressed clean energy operators.

| Company | Ticker | Group | EV/Sales | EV/Gross Profit | EV/ARR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stem, Inc. | STEM | Subject | 2.4x | 6.3x | 6.2x |
| Fluence Energy | FLNC | Clean energy software | ~0.4x | ~3–4x | N/A |
| Itron | ITRI | Smart grid / utility software | ~2.0x | ~4–5x | N/A |
| Landis+Gyr | LAND.SW | Utility metering software | ~1.2x | ~3–4x | N/A |
| Sunrun | RUN | Distressed clean energy | ~2.0x | ~6–7x | N/A |
| SunPower | SPWR | Distressed (reorganising) | Not meaningful | Not meaningful | N/A |

*Peer multiples are approximate estimates based on publicly available market data at the May 2026 snapshot date. EV/ARR is not disclosed in standard form by any peer listed; Fluence Energy is hardware-heavy with thin gross margins, which suppresses its EV/Sales relative to software-oriented peers.*

The table reveals an uncomfortable truth: on EV/Sales, Stem already trades at a premium to Fluence Energy and in line with Itron — companies with substantially larger installed bases and more predictable revenue streams. On EV/Gross Profit, Stem's 6.3x sits broadly in line with Sunrun's distressed-but-stabilised range, though Sunrun's complex lease-backed asset portfolio distorts the comparison. The implication is that Stem has been partially re-rated toward software comps already — a remarkable distance from the delisting notice it received in August 2024 — but the re-rating rests on continued ARR growth and EBITDA progression rather than on current-period fundamentals that would justify these levels on their own.

## What the Current Price Is Pricing In

At $9.72 per share and a $377 million enterprise value, the market is applying approximately 6.2x to trailing ARR of $61.1 million and roughly 5.6x to the forward ARR guidance midpoint of $67.5 million. These are multiples consistent with early-stage SaaS companies demonstrating 15–20 percent ARR growth — not with distressed industrial operators. The implied bet is specific: that Stem's ARR reaches approximately $90–100 million within two to three years, adjusted EBITDA sustains above $15 million, and the $68 million convertible maturing in December 2028 can be refinanced or retired without triggering another equity-dilutive restructuring.

Every quarter of underperformance erodes the option value embedded in the share price. Cash burned $12.3 million in a single quarter through March 2026, and total liabilities of $547.8 million exceed total assets of ~~$308.9 million~~ ==$281.9 million== by approximately ~~$239 million~~ ==$266 million==. The $30 million at-the-money equity programme established in March 2026, while undrawn at quarter-end, signals that management acknowledges the equity may need to absorb near-term funding gaps — and every share issued dilutes the per-share value of any eventual software re-rating.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

Constructing explicit valuation scenarios requires projecting ARR to end-2027, applying scenario-appropriate multiples, and netting estimated debt. PIK compounding on the $134 million senior secured notes at 12 percent is assumed to push that tranche to approximately $158 million by end-2027; combined with $187 million in convertibles and estimated cash of $15–20 million, net debt at that point could reach $325–345 million depending on cash burn trajectory. The ATM programme introduces meaningful dilution risk in adverse scenarios, assumed to add approximately one million shares in the base case and three million in the bear case.

| Scenario | ARR end-2027 | Multiple | Implied EV | Est. Net Debt | Equity Value | Per Share (~10–12.5M shares) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bull** | $90M | 6.0x EV/ARR | $540M | ~$325M | ~$215M | ~$20.50 |
| **Base** | $70M | 3.5x EV/ARR | $245M | ~$330M | ~($85M) | Near zero |
| **Bear** | $55M | 1.5x EV/ARR | $83M | ~$345M | ~($262M) | Zero |

*Bull: EBITDA inflects to $25M+, PowerTrack EMS wins 3+ major utility contracts, ATM minimally drawn. Base: ARR in line with guidance, EBITDA reaches $12M, hardware modest, ATM partially drawn. Bear: Q2–Q3 2026 revenue misses guidance low, cash falls below $20M by year-end, ATM substantially drawn.*

The scenario table encapsulates the essential character of Stem's equity: it is a binary outcome dressed in the costume of a going concern. The bull case yields a share price roughly double the current level; the base case — ARR growing precisely in line with management guidance — still implies equity destruction because a 3.5x multiple applied to $70 million of ARR generates only $245 million of enterprise value, less than the estimated $330 million in net debt. The current $9.72 price is therefore best understood not as a measured mid-range estimate but as a market-implied probability-weighted option, assigning roughly 35–45 percent probability to the bull scenario while accepting near-zero recovery in all others.

## Historical Multiple Range and the Re-Rating Roadmap

The distance Stem has already travelled is instructive. At its SPAC listing in April 2021, the stock briefly implied an enterprise value approaching $2 billion — roughly 10x forward revenue projections at a moment when clean energy enthusiasm overwhelmed fundamental diligence. By August 2024, after the hardware implosion, the guidance evisceration, and the NYSE delisting notice, the stock traded below $1.00 pre-split: the equity was pricing in near-zero going-concern optionality, with the EV essentially representing the outstanding debt discounted for default probability rather than any software franchise value.

The recovery to $9.72 — a 52-week gain of approximately 58 percent from depressed lows — reflects a partial re-rating driven by three tangible milestones: the June 2025 debt exchange ~~extending all material maturities past 2028~~ ==extending the majority of long-dated maturities to 2030 while leaving the $68 million 2028 convertibles outstanding==, the first-ever positive adjusted EBITDA validating the margin thesis, and 16 percent ARR growth demonstrating that the recurring software base is real and expanding. Seven sell-side analysts covering Stem maintained a consensus Hold rating with an average 12-month price target of $13.08, implying approximately 35 percent upside — a target that embeds modest ARR acceleration and continued EBITDA improvement without requiring a transformational catalyst.

For a full re-rating toward clean-energy-software-comp multiples — Itron-like EV/Sales of 2x or better sustained — the company would need at least three consecutive quarters of ARR growth above 20 percent, adjusted EBITDA sustained above $15 million on a trailing basis, and a credible path to retiring or refinancing the 2028 convertible without dilutive equity issuance. PowerTrack EMS utility contract wins — particularly any multi-year managed-services agreements with regulated utilities — would be the single most powerful re-rating catalyst, transforming the revenue profile from software-adjacent to demonstrably recurring in analyst models. Until that evidence accumulates, Stem trades where distressed companies with credible software assets always trade: at a discount to where the thesis could take it, pricing the probability of success rather than the success itself.

chapters.title: Earnings Story: The Quarterly Cadence From Hardware Collapse to Software Ramp
chapters.body:
## From Hardware Trough to Software Thesis

The most arresting chart in Stem's investor materials is not the ARR line or the cash balance — it is the gross margin waterfall from 2020 to the present. ~~GAAP gross margin ran negative in every fiscal year through 2024,~~ ==GAAP gross margin was negative in FY2020 and again in FY2024, sandwiching thin positive prints in FY2021 through FY2023,== a structural artifact of a capital-intensive hardware resale business that deferred costs while recognising revenue at commissioning. By full-year 2024, as hardware volume collapsed and delayed write-downs cleared, GAAP gross margin still sat at negative 7.6 percent on $144.6 million in revenue. By full-year 2025, that same metric had crossed 38 percent positive. Forty-six percentage points of GAAP gross margin recovery in twelve months is the earnings story that management is trying to tell — and that a cautious analyst community is still in the process of believing.

## The Hardware Collapse Quarters: 2024

Fiscal 2024 began on the heels of a deliberate and painful strategy reset. Revenue fell 69 percent year-over-year to $144.6 million, from a base of roughly $466 million in fiscal 2023, when large-scale battery hardware resale dominated the top line. The company simultaneously absorbed an NYSE delisting notice in August 2024, after its 30-day average stock price fell below $1.00, adding a capital markets crisis to an operational one.

The revenue collapse was architectural, not competitive. Stem stopped pursuing large-scale hardware resale contracts that had generated outsized top-line figures but contributed negative gross margin on a GAAP basis. Hardware revenue that once ran in the hundreds of millions was reduced to a residual by late 2024. The software and services base that remained — then representing perhaps 25–30 percent of the legacy revenue mix — was not yet large enough to fill the void. Full-year 2024 GAAP gross profit was negative $11.1 million.

By the time Arun Narayanan succeeded David Buzby as chief executive on January 27, 2025, he inherited a company with a cleared strategic direction but a deeply stressed balance sheet and a sell-side community whose credibility had been badly damaged by the August 2024 guidance collapse — from an implied $617 million midpoint to $144.6 million in actuals, one of the largest revenue guidance reductions in the clean energy sector in recent years.

## The Proof-of-Concept Year: 2025

Fiscal 2025 validated the margin thesis. Revenue from the core software, services, and edge-hardware segment reached $141.4 million, growing 25 percent year-over-year; total company revenue, including approximately $15 million in opportunistic hardware resale, came to roughly $156 million. GAAP gross profit reached $60.0 million — a reversal of $71 million in gross margin dollars in a single year. Non-GAAP gross margins ran between 40 and 49 percent across the year's quarters.

Two structural actions shaped the income statement. The April 2025 workforce reduction — approximately 27 percent of headcount, from roughly 480 to 350 employees — incurred $6.1 million in restructuring charges but was projected to deliver approximately $30 million in annualised 2026 savings. The June 2025 debt exchange retired approximately $350 million of convertible notes in exchange for $155 million of new 11 percent first-lien senior secured notes and $10 million in cash, eliminating near-term maturity pressure at the cost of a higher cash interest burden.

The year's most significant statistical milestone arrived with the full-year results: Stem reported its first-ever positive adjusted EBITDA of $6.7 million, and its first-ever positive operating cash flow of $6.9 million. The GAAP net income figure of $137.8 million for fiscal 2025 requires careful reading — it reflects almost entirely the ~~$195 million~~ ==$220.0 million== debt extinguishment gain from the June exchange, not operations. Operating loss for the year was approximately $55 million; that is the honest baseline for the ongoing business.

Annual recurring revenue — the cleanest proxy for software scale — reached $61.1 million at December 31, 2025, growing 16 percent year-over-year. The ARR base reflects contractual renewals primarily from PowerTrack APM solar monitoring subscriptions, PowerTrack Optimizer dispatch licences, and growing contributions from PowerBidder Pro market participation fees. Management's fiscal 2026 ARR guidance of $65–70 million implies 6–15 percent growth from the year-end base, consistent with the prior year's rate rather than an acceleration.

## Q1 2026: The First Miss

The first quarter of 2026, reported May 6, was the first substantive test of investor confidence in the recovery narrative — and fell short. Revenue of $29.0 million was down 11 percent year-over-year, reflecting continued hardware wind-down that outpaced software ramp. GAAP gross margin held at 37.4 percent, consistent with the software-weighted mix, but operating loss widened to $14.2 million and net loss reached $18.9 million. Cash declined $12.3 million in the quarter, ending at $36.6 million.

| Period | Revenue | GAAP Gross Margin | Operating Loss | Cash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2024 (full year) | $144.6M | (7.6%) | ~$(100M)+ | — |
| FY2025 (full year) | ~$156M | 38.0% | ~$(55M) | — |
| Q1 2026 | $29.0M | 37.4% | $(14.2M) | $36.6M |

The arithmetic from Q1 is uncomfortable. Achieving the fiscal 2026 guidance midpoint of $165 million requires $136 million across the remaining three quarters — an average of approximately $45.3 million per quarter, representing roughly 56 percent sequential growth from Q1's $29.0 million base. Even the guidance floor of $140 million demands approximately $37 million per quarter across Q2–Q4. Neither trajectory is arithmetically impossible given the hardware resale lumpiness — management guided approximately $40 million in opportunistic hardware resale for fiscal 2026, which could concentrate in a single quarter — and the expected PowerTrack EMS revenue ramp in the second half. But neither is visible in Q1's run rate.

The guidance range's unusual $50 million width on approximately $165 million of midpoint revenue signals genuine uncertainty about the pace of software bookings conversion and hardware resale timing. Software and services revenue growing at 25 percent year-over-year from the $141 million FY2025 base would imply roughly $176 million from core operations alone — but only if the hardware resale contribution materialises at the guided $40 million level.

## ARR Trajectory and What the Math Requires

The $61.1 million ARR at year-end 2025, growing at 16 percent annually, is the building block for any sustained bull case on Stem. Extrapolating that rate produces approximately $95 million in ARR by year-end 2028 (with roughly $82 million reached by year-end 2027) — a level at which the software base would generate roughly $36–40 million in gross profit at current margins. That remains short of the cash interest burden on $155 million of 11 percent senior secured notes, without accounting for the $183.8 million in convertible notes maturing in 2028 and 2030.

| Period | ARR | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2024 (implied) | ~$52.7M | — |
| FY2025 | $61.1M | +16% |
| FY2026 guidance | $65–70M | +6–15% |

The FY2026 ARR guide implies net adds of approximately $4–9 million. PowerTrack EMS, the utility-scale storage control product launched in September 2025, is the most plausible source of ARR step-up — but recognised revenue from EMS deployments is not expected to register meaningfully until late 2026 or early 2027, given project commissioning timelines. The $65–70 million guide therefore reflects primarily the existing contractual base, not yet a demonstrable new-product contribution. Net revenue retention from the AlsoEnergy-derived APM monitoring base remains the foundation; new logo adds from PowerTrack Optimizer and PowerBidder Pro supply the incremental growth.

## The Analyst Credibility Problem

Seven analysts cover Stem as of the frozen snapshot date, all at Hold with an average 12-month price target of $13.08 — approximately 35 percent above the May 2026 market price near $9.72. The consensus Hold is not a vote of no-confidence in the transformation; it is a vote of insufficient evidence accumulated against a backdrop of damaged credibility.

For an upgrade cycle to materialise, analysts need at minimum two consecutive quarters of ARR growth at or above the 16 percent annual rate, operating cash flow neutrality outside of one-time items, and visible PowerTrack EMS bookings converting to a discernible 2027 revenue line. A first-ever positive adjusted EBITDA of $6.7 million for fiscal 2025 was a necessary first step; it was not sufficient to move consensus from Hold to Buy while cash was declining $12 million per quarter and total liabilities of $548 million were balanced against ~~$309 million~~ ==$282 million== in assets.

The $30 million ATM equity programme established in March 2026 — with no shares drawn by quarter-end — is the most visible signal of management's own risk calculus. Its existence acknowledges that the current trajectory does not self-fund. Until the ARR line shows acceleration meaningfully above the 16 percent baseline and quarterly cash burn narrows toward zero, the earnings story remains a thesis in progress rather than a thesis confirmed.

chapters.title: Leadership: The SLB Network, the AlsoEnergy CFO, and a Board Built for Restructuring
chapters.body:
## The Architect Who Crossed the Sector Lines

When Stem's board went searching for a permanent chief executive in late 2024, the brief was specific: find someone who had built AI-driven software platforms for physical asset operations, had managed enterprise-scale digital transformations, and understood renewable energy well enough to speak credibly to project developers and utilities. Arun Narayanan, appointed on January 27, 2025, met each criterion, but what made his hire unusual was the sequence — a career arc that read less like a résumé and more like a compound-interest equation.

Narayanan spent 21 years at SLB (formerly Schlumberger), the global oilfield services giant, rising to Vice President of Data and Analytics in the Software division. The relevance was not the oil-and-gas context but the discipline: SLB's software arm was building industrial IoT and AI/ML platforms for physical asset optimization years before "AI-driven dispatch" entered the energy storage lexicon. The work required integrating telemetry from distributed field assets — wells, compressors, pressure sensors — into predictive models capable of making real-time operational recommendations at scale. When Stem describes PowerTrack Optimizer as an AI engine that ingests grid pricing, weather forecasts, and battery telemetry to dispatch energy assets, the infrastructure problem is structurally identical.

The second chapter of Narayanan's career compounded that foundation at a different scale. As Chief Data Officer at Anglo American, the London-listed global mining company, from January 2018 to June 2023, he led a digital transformation program across operations spanning copper, iron ore, and platinum — geographically dispersed, operationally complex, capital-intensive. The discipline of enterprise-scale change management — convincing operating teams to trust algorithmic recommendations over intuition, retraining workflows around software decision-support — is precisely what Stem requires as it asks 16,000 commercial solar customers to migrate from legacy monitoring tools to an integrated AI platform.

The third chapter brought the sector directly into frame. Narayanan joined RES (Renewable Energy Systems) as Chief Digital Officer in August 2023, then assumed the role of CEO of RES Digital Solutions in April 2024, positioning him at the intersection of renewable energy project development and digital software infrastructure. By the time Stem approached him, his résumé described a deliberate apprenticeship for exactly this job: industrial AI from SLB, enterprise transformation from Anglo American, renewable software from RES.

## The AlsoEnergy CFO, Now Managing the Asset He Helped Price

If Narayanan's hire reflected the board's theory of the growth case, the appointment of Brian Musfeldt as CFO on July 17, 2025, reflected something more precise: an acknowledgment that Stem's central financial problem was also its central strategic asset.

Musfeldt brought nearly 30 years of clean technology finance experience to the role, but his most consequential credential was institutional memory. He served as CFO of AlsoEnergy before its acquisition by Stem ~~in January 2022 for approximately $695 million in stock~~ ==on February 1, 2022, announced at approximately $695 million in roughly 75% cash and 25% stock, with a final purchase price of about $652 million== — a transaction that has since come to look dramatically overpriced relative to Stem's current market capitalization of roughly $93 million. Musfeldt was on the sell side of that deal. He understood the AlsoEnergy business — its customer relationships, its SaaS architecture, its operational cost structure, its revenue quality — in the granular detail that only a sitting finance chief possesses.

The strategic inference is significant. The AlsoEnergy acquisition created what is now PowerTrack APM, the solar monitoring and performance analytics platform serving approximately 16,000 C&I customers across more than 30 gigawatts in over 50 countries. That platform is Stem's most defensible recurring revenue asset and the foundation of its $61.1 million ARR base. Whether Musfeldt's appointment represents institutional continuity or a deliberate choice to have the architect of the acquired company's finances manage the restructuring, the practical effect is identical: the CFO has direct knowledge of Stem's most valuable software asset at the level of its original architecture and customer economics.

Managing that asset now requires navigating $548 million in total liabilities against ~~$309 million~~ ==$281.9 million== in assets, cash of $36.6 million as of March 31, 2026 declining at roughly $12 million per quarter, and a $30 million at-the-market equity program established in March 2026. The ATM program is a loaded signal: it communicates that management considers dilutive equity raises a live scenario, even as Narayanan describes a path to adjusted EBITDA profitability of $10–15 million for FY2026. Musfeldt's role is to maintain credibility in both narratives simultaneously.

## A Board Built for Restructuring Scenarios

The board composition assembled around Narayanan bears the specific signatures of a company scenario-planning beyond its base case.

David Buzby, who served as Interim CEO from mid-2024 through January 2025 and remains as non-executive Chairman, carries a 35-year renewable energy career including tenure as CEO of SunEdison. His stabilization of Stem through the August 2024 NYSE delisting notice and the guidance restatement was essential, and his continuity as Chairman provides institutional memory of the crisis period. The governance question his earlier dual role created — simultaneously running the company while chairing the board charged with overseeing management — was resolved with Narayanan's appointment and formalized in December 2025 when Narayanan was added as a Class I Director, expanding the board from seven to eight members. CEO and Chairman are now formally distinct roles.

The March 2025 additions of Krishna Shivram and Vasudevan Guruswamy, seven weeks after Narayanan's appointment, revealed the shape of the board he wanted around him.

Shivram, Managing Partner at Veritec Capital Partners and former CFO of Weatherford International, brings a specific form of institutional knowledge: Weatherford itself executed a Chapter 11 restructuring in 2019, and Shivram's tenure as its CFO gave him direct experience managing a company through balance-sheet stress, debt negotiation, and post-restructuring operational recovery. His appointment to Stem's board — which occurred before the June 2025 debt exchange that retired $195 million in principal — is the clearest signal that the board was stress-testing scenarios beyond consensual exchange. Appointing a director with Chapter 11 experience is not standard governance practice for a company confident its base case will play out cleanly.

Guruswamy's profile is different but complementary. His background at SLB in cloud SaaS and data infrastructure connects him directly to Narayanan's professional network and gives the board a technology-side validator for the PowerTrack platform architecture and product roadmap decisions. The alignment between Narayanan's SLB pedigree and Guruswamy's SLB background is not coincidental; it reflects a deliberate pattern of board composition mirroring the CEO's epistemic framework.

## Angeleno Group, Tyson, and the Capital Allocation Question

Anil Tammineedi, representing Angeleno Group on Stem's board, is a quieter but structurally significant presence. Angeleno Group is a clean energy-focused private equity firm that has been a Stem investor since the company's early SPAC-era capital raises. A board seat provides direct visibility into capital allocation decisions — including the ATM program's parameters and the terms of any future equity raise.

The relevant question for sophisticated observers is whether Angeleno's presence creates alignment or tension with public shareholders around the pace and terms of dilutive equity issuance. Private equity sponsors in a distressed equity scenario often have different optimization functions than index fund holders; the board composition gives Angeleno direct access to those decision points at a moment when Stem's cash trajectory makes additional issuance a plausible near-term event.

Laura D'Andrea Tyson — Distinguished Professor at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business and former Director of the National Economic Council under President Clinton — is an anomalous presence for a company at Stem's current market capitalization. Her value is unlikely to reside in audit committee oversight. It resides in Washington access and regulatory credibility at a moment when Stem's community solar and utility-scale customers are navigating IRA implementation, USDA grant programs, and interconnection policy. The guidance collapse of 2024 was partly attributable to USDA funding delays; Tyson's policy network functions as a structural hedge against the regulatory-political risks that have demonstrably damaged Stem's revenue forecasting credibility before.

## Compensation as Theory of the Case

The proxy statement filed for the 2025 annual meeting provides the sharpest available signal of what the board is actually demanding from Narayanan. His compensation structure includes equity awards tied to ARR growth targets and adjusted EBITDA milestones rather than total revenue scale — a calibration that reflects the board's understanding that the old revenue metric, which ballooned toward $500 million on hardware resale before collapsing 69 percent in a single year, is a poor proxy for business quality. Tying long-term incentive compensation to ARR and EBITDA aligns the CEO's payout directly with the software transformation thesis: grow the recurring base, prove the margin model, generate operating cash. If Narayanan hits the board's ARR milestones, the software business is demonstrably viable. If he misses them, the equity is underwater regardless of how the hardware wind-down is packaged. The incentive structure is, in this sense, the board's most transparent statement of its theory of the case — and its most direct admission of what the prior regime's revenue metric had obscured.

chapters.title: Customers and Markets: The C&I Solar Core, the Utility-Scale Frontier, and the EMEA Bet
chapters.body:
## The C&I Solar Foundation: 16,000 Customers, One Inherited Platform

The bedrock of Stem's customer franchise is a legacy it acquired, not organically built. When the company paid ~~approximately $695 million in stock for AlsoEnergy Holdings in January 2022~~ ==a final purchase price of approximately $652 million for AlsoEnergy Holdings on February 1, 2022 in a mix of roughly 75 percent cash and 25 percent stock (announced at $695 million)==, the strategic rationale centred less on immediate financial synergy than on installed base: AlsoEnergy brought roughly 16,000 commercial and industrial solar operators onto a single monitoring and performance analytics platform, representing more than 30 gigawatts of capacity spread across more than 50 countries. By early 2026, that installed base — now served by PowerTrack APM — had become the most defensible element of Stem's portfolio, generating subscription revenue that is simultaneously diversified and sticky.

The diversity is structural. Across 16,000 accounts ranging from retail property owners with rooftop arrays to industrial manufacturers managing multi-site solar programmes, no single customer or narrow cohort can impair revenues materially. That distribution provides stability rare in early-stage enterprise software, but it carries a corresponding constraint: upsell velocity is throttled by the sheer heterogeneity of the base. Thirteen of the top fifteen US commercial and industrial solar operators use the platform, and that cohort — larger, financially sophisticated, managing portfolio-scale deployments — represents the natural funnel toward PowerTrack Optimizer dispatch contracts and PowerBidder Pro wholesale market participation.

## Community Solar: The IRA-Amplified Revenue Pool

Within the APM base, community solar has emerged as a structurally privileged sub-segment. Stem's claim of serving 90 percent of leading US community solar asset owners reflects both AlsoEnergy's historical concentration in this vertical and the absence of a credible alternative at scale. Community solar projects — shared solar gardens through which subscribers receive bill credits proportional to their ownership stake — require meticulous performance tracking and granular billing data, functions PowerTrack APM was purpose-built to provide.

The Inflation Reduction Act materially enlarged the addressable market. The law extended and enhanced the Section 48 investment tax credit for community solar projects, maintained 30 percent base credits through 2032, and introduced low-income community adders that unlocked new project economics for developers targeting underserved markets. Wood Mackenzie estimated in mid-2025 that the IRA's community solar provisions would support cumulative US deployments of 10–15 gigawatts through 2030 — roughly double the pre-IRA trajectory. At a representative software contract of $15,000–$25,000 in annual recurring revenue per community solar project, a 3,000-project incremental base from IRA-driven growth would imply $45–75 million of additional ARR opportunity relative to Stem's current $61.1 million total ARR base. Capture will depend on competitive intensity and whether Stem's dominant position holds against software entrants specifically targeting the community solar vertical.

## BESS Dispatch and the Utility-Scale Frontier

Battery energy storage dispatch optimization represents a qualitatively richer revenue tier than APM monitoring alone. PowerTrack Optimizer — the successor brand to the original Athena engine — applies continuous machine-learning dispatch decisions across approximately 2 gigawatt-hours of storage assets under management, balancing demand-charge reduction, energy arbitrage, and ancillary services participation in real time. Dispatch-optimised storage contracts typically carry higher ARR per asset than monitoring-only APM subscriptions, reflecting the measurable revenue generation that optimised dispatch delivers to storage owners.

The utility-scale segment introduces a structurally different customer profile: independent power producers, large energy developers, and EPC contractors controlling pipelines of hundreds of megawatts. ~~Stem won its first standalone battery energy storage system project in Nebraska in 2025, a reference win for PowerTrack EMS — the utility-scale energy management system launched in September of that year.~~ ==The first publicly sourced utility-scale selection of PowerTrack EMS — the energy management system launched in September 2025 — was Everyray's 100 megawatt-hour announcement in Germany on March 4, 2026.== Customer concentration risk in this tier is the mirror image of the C&I dynamic: a handful of large IPPs and EPC contractors control substantial order flow, making a single large contract disproportionately valuable and a single loss disproportionately damaging. Management has been explicit that PowerTrack EMS revenue recognition is not expected to be meaningful until late 2026 or early 2027, reflecting the longer procurement, permitting, and commissioning cycles of grid-scale projects.

## The IRA Storage Buildout: Tax Law as Market Catalyst

The Inflation Reduction Act's provisions on battery storage represent the most direct structural tailwind for Stem's utility-scale software ambitions. Section 48 of the Internal Revenue Code, as amended by the IRA, extended the standalone storage investment tax credit — allowing battery storage to qualify for a 30 percent ITC independent of solar co-location for the first time. The domestic content bonus adds a further 10 percentage points for projects satisfying US manufacturing thresholds for steel, iron, and manufactured components. For a 100 megawatt-hour utility-scale project costing approximately $12–15 million, a 40 percent combined ITC represents $4.8–6 million in tax equity value, a step-change in project IRR that directly accelerates final investment decisions.

BloombergNEF's US battery storage outlook, published in early 2026, projected annual utility-scale installations reaching 30–40 gigawatt-hours per year by 2027–2028 — roughly triple the 2024 installation pace — driven primarily by IRA economics and grid operator interconnection queue clearing. At PowerTrack EMS pricing estimated in the range of $3–7 per kilowatt-hour in annual software fees, a 5 percent market share of a 30 gigawatt-hour annual installation market would imply $45–105 million in incremental annualized software revenue, a potential multiple of Stem's current ARR base. That outcome is achievable only over a multi-year ramp and presupposes competitive win rates that remain unproven at scale.

## Mercuria and the Financial-Operator Buyer

The most strategically significant customer signal in Stem's 2025 commercial disclosures was not a utility renewal or a large APM contract — it was Mercuria's standardization of a second renewable asset portfolio on PowerBidder Pro in Texas. Mercuria is a global commodity trading firm with estimated annual revenues exceeding $120 billion; its selection of a software platform for renewable energy dispatch optimization signals a buyer profile qualitatively unlike the C&I property manager at the base of the APM pyramid.

A commodity trading firm deploying capital across renewable portfolios requires precision dispatch optimization that maximises wholesale market revenue across ERCOT, CAISO, and other organized markets — integrated with trading-desk risk frameworks and capable of processing intraday pricing signals at machine speed. Two California community choice aggregators also signed new PowerBidder Pro contracts in 2025, validating the product's reach into publicly-owned utilities managing ratepayer-funded fleets. Together, these wins suggest PowerBidder Pro is developing credibility in the segment most capable of scaling deployment rapidly: sophisticated financial and institutional operators who can standardize across large asset portfolios rather than negotiating contract by contract.

## EMEA: The Berlin Bet and the Regulatory Asymmetry

Stem's European expansion entered a new phase in ~~Q1 2026~~ ==April 2026== with the $4.3 million ==(389,569 share)== stock acquisition of Vienna-based raicoon GmbH, complementing the previously established Berlin competence centre and the 100 megawatt-hour partnership ~~signed with German developer Everyray in 2025~~ ==with German developer Everyray announced in March 2026==. Together these constitute a deliberate — if capital-light — beachhead in a European market whose grid software dynamics diverge structurally from the United States.

European energy markets operate through capacity mechanisms, balancing markets, and cross-border intraday trading regimes that differ materially from the CAISO or PJM structures PowerTrack's dispatch logic was originally designed to exploit. The German Regelreserve market, the UK Balancing Mechanism, and emerging continental intraday markets each carry distinct bidding rules, settlement windows, and asset certification requirements. Adapting PowerTrack's optimization engine to these regimes demands more than localisation — it requires regulatory and algorithmic re-engineering. The raicoon acquisition was motivated in part by acquiring precisely this competency in the German-speaking markets where battery storage incentives are most developed.

The risk-reward calculus for EMEA is skewed: the capital outlay is minimal — $4.3 million for raicoon, estimated fewer than 30 staff in Berlin — but the potential market is large.
